title: What each text asked
hook: each text asked something different of its readers
tomorrow: so could you staple all these books into one big scripture?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Preacher's quiet house and his first word, remember, before the silver cord. That closed Ecclesiastes. Now the whole shelf, and what each book was asking.
screen: `BEFORE THE SILVER CORD.` → `NOW, THE WHOLE SHELF.`

segments.voice: Someone asks for the short version of a thing that took you years. Give me the summary. One line. The Talmud tells of a man who brought that request to two teachers, one of them Hillel, the sage of Pirkei Avot from a few weeks back, as a dare: teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot. Shammai pushes him away with the builder's measuring rod in his hand. Hillel takes the dare.
screen: `GIVE ME THE ONE-LINE VERSION.` → `THE WHOLE TORAH ON ONE FOOT.` → `HILLEL TAKES THE DARE.`

segments.voice: What is hateful to you, Hillel says, don't do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah. The rest is commentary. Then the odd part: go and learn. Here's the puzzle. If one line is the whole Torah, why send the man off to study? Because in Jewish teaching both are true. The line is real, and it's a door, not the house. Study itself is counted among the commandments; an old teaching in the Mishnah says it equals all the rest together. The commentary is how the line gets lived. Now turn to this shelf and ask each book for its one-foot line. You won't get one answer. The Dhammapada: avoid evil, do good, purify your mind. The Analects: learn, and practice what you learn. The Quran's short surah on time: believe, do good, urge one another to truth and patience. Ecclesiastes: remember now, and eat your bread with joy. Each asks its own, in its own words, of its own people. One to tell a friend tonight: Hillel's famous one-line answer doesn't end at the summary. It ends with an order: go and learn. The puzzle, solved: a summary is where learning starts, and each text's starting line is different.
screen: `WHAT IS HATEFUL TO YOU, DON'T DO.` · `THE REST IS COMMENTARY. GO AND LEARN.` · `A DOOR, NOT THE HOUSE.` · `ASK EACH BOOK FOR ITS LINE.` · then, large: `EACH ASKS ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper and write three short lines, one ask from each of three texts you met on this shelf, in your own words. Read them back slowly. Notice where they ask different things of you, and leave the differences alone.
What each text asked: the one-foot line each book gives, and the learning that goes on past it.
Pocket this one: each asks its own, and a one-line summary is a door, not the house. Talk tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hillel's answer is retold in Jewish teaching as a model of patience and of study: the summary, then 'go and learn'. Readers of several traditions keep a short line from a text as a doorway into the rest of it.

Hillel.meaning: an early sage the Talmud remembers for patience

Shammai.meaning: Hillel's fellow teacher, remembered as the stricter one

Torah.meaning: the Five Books of Moses; also Jewish teaching as a whole

Mishnah.meaning: the early written collection of Jewish oral law

Dhammapada.meaning: a collection of the Buddha's verses

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (the man on one foot; Shammai's measuring rod; Hillel: what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow; the rest is commentary; go and learn)
Mishnah Peah 1:1 (the study of Torah is set against all the other commandments)
Dhammapada 183 (not to commit sin, to do good, to purify one's mind)
Analects 1.1; Quran 103; Ecclesiastes 12:1 and 9:7 (the one-line asks named in the teach)
